articles.title: Traffic Calming Measures Approved for Grimshaw Lane in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Middleton Township Committee has approved a traffic order to enhance safety on Grimshaw Lane, introducing pedestrian crossing islands and reducing on-street parking following concerns over speeding and accidents.
articles.content_html:
Middleton Township Committee has approved a traffic order aimed at improving safety on Grimshaw Lane, a road described as "dangerous" due to a history of speeding and serious accidents, including a fatality. The decision was made during a meeting on September 17, 2026, where the committee greenlit the introduction of three pedestrian crossing islands, the extension of bus stops, and a reduction in on-street parking.

Councillor Dylan Williams, who represents the area and serves as the Rochdale Council portfolio holder for highways and facilities, stated that the initiative has been in the works for four-and-a-half years. He noted that the road layout has been identified as a significant factor contributing to the number of road traffic accidents (RTAs), and the new measures are designed to address these issues. The changes will also include narrowing parts of the road and improving access for disabled individuals at junctions with Shawbury Street, Sedgley Street, and Sandy Lane.

The traffic order was prompted by objections from 11 residents, primarily concerned about the potential loss of parking outside their homes. Despite the objections, Williams reported that the majority of residents consulted were supportive of the proposed changes. The meeting reportedly became heated, reflecting the strong feelings surrounding the parking issue.

The implementation of these traffic calming measures is expected to enhance safety for pedestrians and drivers alike, potentially reducing the risk of further accidents on Grimshaw Lane. The council will now proceed with the necessary arrangements to put the approved measures into effect.

articles.title: Rochdale Secures 2-0 Victory Over Oldham in League Two Derby
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Football Club moved off the bottom of the League Two table with a 2-0 win against Oldham Athletic in a closely contested derby match at Spotland Stadium on September 19, 2026.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Football Club lifted themselves off the bottom of the League Two table with a decisive 2-0 victory against Oldham Athletic in their Greater Manchester derby on September 19, 2026, at Spotland Stadium.

The home side took an early lead just seven minutes into the match. A combination between Charlie Tasker and Jonny Smith down the right flank resulted in Tasker delivering a low cross that was expertly finished by Dan Moss, who swept the ball into the roof of the net.

Oldham had a chance to equalise when forward Mike Fondop missed a clear opportunity in the 25th minute, sliding the ball wide of the post with an open goal at his mercy after a mistake from Rochdale goalkeeper Nils Ramming. The visitors continued to press for an equaliser after the break, but their efforts were thwarted by a resolute Rochdale defence.

Rochdale sealed their victory with a second goal in the 62nd minute. A kick from Oldham goalkeeper Matt Hudson was intercepted by Baba Adeeko, who headed the ball forward for Dajaune Brown. Brown advanced into the penalty area, sidestepped a defender, and fired a powerful shot into the bottom corner, securing the three points for Rochdale.

articles.title: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish to Host Outdoor Service on September 20
articles.excerpt: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish will host an outdoor service on September 20 at 10.30am, followed by refreshments. A new youth group, Roots, will also start on September 20.
articles.content_html:
St Luke’s Church in Deeplish will hold a service of Morning Praise on Sunday, September 20, at 10.30am, weather permitting. The service will take place in the church car park, providing a relaxed atmosphere for attendees of all ages and backgrounds. Following the service, refreshments including tea, coffee, and cake will be available for those who wish to stay and chat.

Reader Sue Horobin will officiate the Morning Praise service, which aims to welcome both regular members and newcomers to the congregation. The church encourages anyone interested in learning more about its activities to join the service, which has no dress code and is designed to be informal and friendly.

In addition to the outdoor service, St Luke’s Church will also host a Bible study group on Wednesday, September 23, at 10am. This group is open to anyone who wishes to explore the Bible in a welcoming environment. Later that day, another Morning Praise service will be held at 11am, officiated by Revd Natty Gray.

Starting on the same day, September 20, a new youth group called Roots will be launched at St Saviour's Church. This group is aimed at school children in Years 6 to 9 and will run every other Sunday from 4pm to 5.30pm. Participants can expect fun games, activities, and discussions about the Bible with peers. For more information about the youth group or church activities, interested individuals can contact the church office.

The Heywood Community Gala, which took place from 18 to 20 September at The Pig and Whistle, has come under scrutiny after photos from the event showed a significantly smaller setup than the colourful promotional material suggested. The event was advertised as featuring large fairground rides, live music, street food, and children's entertainment, but images released on Saturday morning depicted only a handful of gazebos outside the venue, with no large rides in sight.

The promotional artwork, generated by AI, depicted a vibrant scene with performers, balloons, and crowds, leading to comparisons on social media with Glasgow's infamous Willy Wonka experience, which faced similar criticism in 2024 for not meeting expectations. A Facebook page, Cameron Boland - Scam Event Watch & Awareness, has been vocal in its criticism of the Heywood event, alleging it was a scam and questioning the adequacy of security and entertainment arrangements.

Cameron Boland, the organiser, has been accused of mismanaging previous events, including a similar gala that was cancelled by Salford City Council and Greater Manchester Police in August. While the Facebook page has raised concerns about the gala's setup, including claims that performers were situated on a rug between tables, these allegations have not been independently verified. The photographs from the event do show activity taking place, but they do not provide a complete picture of what was available throughout the three-day event.

Kelly, the tenant and operator of The Pig and Whistle, defended the event, stating that it was still ongoing and that there were activities planned for the remainder of the weekend. The situation has raised questions about the expectations set by promotional materials versus the actual experience provided, highlighting the importance of transparency in event advertising.

articles.title: Rochdale MP Paul Waugh Highlights Local Achievements as Minister for Early Education
articles.excerpt: Paul Waugh, Rochdale's MP and Minister for Early Education, discusses local initiatives and funding aimed at improving children's services and community engagement in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Paul Waugh, the Member of Parliament for Rochdale, has shared insights into his role as Minister for Early Education, highlighting recent initiatives that aim to benefit local children and families. In a recent article, Waugh reflected on his experiences visiting various community organisations in Rochdale, including KYP, BACP, and Aspire 2 Inspire, where he observed the positive impact of the Government's Holiday Activities and Food programme during the summer holidays.

Waugh emphasised the importance of providing children with a strong start in life, noting that the programme offered local youngsters nutritious meals and engaging activities. He also visited the Best Start Family Hub on Derby Street in Heywood, one of seventeen hubs across the borough that support families from pregnancy through early childhood. Waugh expressed his commitment to expanding these vital services, stating that they make a significant difference in the community.

Additionally, Waugh discussed the £20 million Pride in Place funding allocated to Smallbridge, Hurstead, and Belfield over the next decade. He has been actively engaging with local residents to gather their input on how to best utilise these funds, ensuring that the community has a say in shaping their environment. Waugh's approach reflects a commitment to empowering local voices and addressing the needs of the community.

As part of his ministerial duties, Waugh is currently representing the UK at UNESCO's Digital Learning Week in Paris, where education ministers from around the world are discussing the integration of artificial intelligence in education. Waugh's dual focus on local engagement and international collaboration illustrates his dedication to both Rochdale and the broader educational landscape.

articles.title: Kashmir Youth Project Marks Year of Community Achievements in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: The Kashmir Youth Project celebrated a successful year of community engagement, reporting over 11,000 interactions and significant financial gains for local residents during its annual meeting.
articles.content_html:
Members, volunteers, partners, staff and community supporters gathered to celebrate the achievements of the Kashmir Youth Project (KYP) during its annual general and public meetings held on 19 September 2026. The event highlighted the impact KYP has made across Rochdale over the past year, showcasing its commitment to community welfare and support.

Throughout the year 2025/26, KYP recorded 11,259 engagements and visits across its various services, which include advice and welfare, learning and skills, adult day care, and a community food pantry. The organisation collaborated with over 80 agencies, delivering more than 200 community events and activities aimed at strengthening partnerships and creating opportunities for local residents.

KYP's efforts have resulted in significant financial and social value for the community, securing £2 million in financial gains for residents through 3,526 client interventions. These interventions provided essential advice, guidance, and support to those in need, demonstrating the organisation's vital role in the local area.

The expansion of KYP's Advice and Welfare Outreach locations has further enhanced its reach, increasing from five to 11 centres across Rochdale, Heywood, and Middleton. This growth allows KYP to assist more residents in accessing the necessary services and opportunities to improve their lives. Additionally, the organisation delivered 8,460 learning hours and supported 164 individuals in pursuing further training and employment.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky cleft known as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of local storytelling — but the supernatural claims rest in folklore, not in official records.
articles.summary: The rocky cleft known as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of local storytelling — but the supernatural claims rest in folklore, not in official records.
articles.body:
Healey Dell sits where the River Spodden squeezes through a narrow gorge known locally as the Thrutch, a shady, waterfall‑scattered hollow two miles north of Rochdale town centre. Today it is a council‑managed nature reserve with a heritage centre, tea rooms and family trails; the long stone viaduct that towers above the gorge is a Grade II listed structure and the Dell is promoted as a place of industrial archaeology and wild beauty. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The name “Fairies’ Chapel” points to one of the Dell’s most persistent stories: a pocket of hollowed rock that, to Victorian and earlier visitors, looked like a tiny church with a pulpit and seats carved by the water. Local guidebooks and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre explain that the “chapel” is essentially a water‑worn niche in the rock — a natural feature shaped by erosion rather than human carving. That explanation sits alongside the telling that a great summer storm in the 1830s changed the Spodden’s course and altered or buried parts of the formation people once pointed to. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

Where the written history stops, folklore gathers. The most often‑repeated version appears in nineteenth‑century collections of Lancashire tales: the Fairies’ Chapel becomes the stage for tricks, warnings and moral tales involving fairies, witches, prophetic “Fairy Queens” and local characters such as millers and gentry. Robert Roby’s Lancashire Legends (a Victorian compilation that survives in full online) gives a long, theatrical account in which a narrow rocky hollow is haunted by “the good people,” encounters with enchanted hares and strange lights, and episodes of bewitchment and retribution. These are literary and oral traditions rather than records of events that can be checked against archives. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Later local retellings and the Dell’s own heritage material mix Roby’s account with other regional motifs: witches turned to stone by a Fairy King, a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden, and love stories involving the Byron and Chadwick families. These stories are clearly labelled as legend by the heritage centre and by council information aimed at visitors; they help explain why the spot became one of the Dell’s most evocative attractions, but they are not supported by contemporary documentary evidence of supernatural events. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

That distinction matters. The documented facts are straightforward: Healey Dell is an historically important landscape (with a listed viaduct and remnants of mills) and it is managed as a local nature reserve. The physical rock features people called the Fairies’ Chapel are the result of ordinary geological and fluvial action; floods and industrial change have altered the appearance of the Dell since at least the early nineteenth century. Claims that fairies, witches or a Fairy King literally created or inhabit the chapel are part of oral tradition and folklore — rich, culturally valuable stories, but not verifiable historical fact. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

If you come looking for fairies, the sensible local advice is to bring imagination and respect. The Dell’s folklore is part of what makes it special: the stories connect people across generations to place and to the Dell’s industrial and natural past. If you want the clearest separation between what’s recorded and what’s told, read the nineteenth‑century legends as folklore, and the council and heritage centre material as the place’s recorded history and practical visitor information. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Bottom line: there is nothing in the official record to confirm supernatural activity at the Fairies’ Chapel — only enduring, well‑documented local stories that have been collected, retold and celebrated by authors and by the Healey Dell community. The chapel is best enjoyed as a meeting point of geology, industrial archaeology and imagination — a small landscape where the boundary between history and legend is part of the attraction. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Launches Resilient Roch Flood Resilience Programme
articles.excerpt: The Resilient Roch programme aims to enhance flood resilience in vulnerable communities across Rochdale, focusing on building trust and partnerships to address climate risks.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has launched the Resilient Roch programme, an innovative initiative designed to improve flood and climate resilience among households and communities at risk of flooding. This project is delivered in partnership with the National Flood Forum and is funded by the Flood and Coastal Innovation Programme (FCIP).

The Resilient Roch programme specifically targets disadvantaged and diverse neighbourhoods that have historically been vulnerable to flooding. The initiative aims to enhance community preparedness and adaptation by integrating flood resilience with broader issues such as housing, health, and climate awareness. This approach is particularly important in Rochdale, which has experienced significant flooding events, including the major floods caused by Storm Eva in 2015.

Rather than relying on traditional consultation methods, the programme adopts a relationship-first approach, focusing on building trust through long-term engagement with residents, community organisations, schools, and local stakeholders. This model aims to reach those most vulnerable to flooding, including marginalised communities and non-English speakers, who often face barriers to participation in such initiatives.

Key objectives of the Resilient Roch programme include improving flood literacy, increasing the uptake of property flood resilience measures, and fostering community ownership of flood preparedness. The project also seeks to strengthen partnerships between residents, local authorities, and other stakeholders to create lasting resilience and enhance community capacity. As the programme progresses, it is expected to significantly contribute to the overall safety and wellbeing of Rochdale's communities.

articles.content_html:
Ofsted has published a new inspection report for Tooth, Jessica Lena, a childcare provider in Rochdale, dated 18 September 2026. The report outlines the findings from the recent inspection and includes any ratings awarded to the provider.

Settings registered on the Early Years Register are typically inspected at least once within a four-year period. Ofsted prioritises inspections and may conduct them more frequently if there are concerns about a provider's performance. Newly registered settings are inspected within 18 months of their registration date.

The report is part of Ofsted's ongoing commitment to ensure quality in early years education and childcare. Parents and guardians can access the report to understand the quality of care and education provided by Tooth, Jessica Lena.

For those interested in further details, the report is available on the Ofsted website, where users can also subscribe for alerts regarding future reports for this provider.

articles.title: New Young Futures Hub to Support Rochdale's Young People
articles.excerpt: A new Young Futures Hub is set to open in Rochdale, providing vital support and opportunities for local youth aged 10 to 25, including mental health services and employment training.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale is set to benefit from a new Young Futures Hub, designed to provide comprehensive support and opportunities for young people in the community. The hub will cater to individuals aged 10 to 18, and up to 25 for those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The initiative will offer a range of services, including mental health support, employment and skills training, sports activities, and crime prevention services. This development is part of the Government's National Youth Strategy, Youth Matters, which aims to address the needs of young people highlighted in a recent survey involving 14,000 participants.

Rochdale Council will also receive assistance through the Local Youth Transformation programme, which aims to enhance leadership, train staff, and foster lasting partnerships within the community. The hub is expected to create a safe and supportive environment for young people, addressing the growing reliance on online interactions and the lack of face-to-face opportunities.

The opening of the Young Futures Hub marks a significant step towards providing holistic support for the youth of Rochdale, ensuring they have access to essential services that promote their well-being and development.

articles.title: Why does Rochdale say 'cruckle'?
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the local verb 'cruckle' — what it means, where it comes from, and why Rochdale people still claim it as their own.
articles.summary: A short guide to the local verb 'cruckle' — what it means, where it comes from, and why Rochdale people still claim it as their own.
articles.body:
If you grew up in parts of Rochdale you will probably recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” Locally, to “cruckle” is used to mean rolling or twisting the ankle — that awkward stumble you can often walk off but which still makes you wince.

That everyday meaning is reflected in recent research into how people label and describe accents and local speech across Greater Manchester. A 2024 perceptual‑dialectology study (draw‑a‑map / keywords method) recorded people naming “cruckle” among the words they associate with Rochdale speech, alongside other locally salient terms such as guinnel (ginnel) and “broad”. The study’s maps and sample (hundreds of contributors from the ten GM boroughs) show that, whether by habit or pride, many respondents link the word specifically to Rochdale.

But “cruckle” is not a brand‑new invention. Historical dialect lexicons record older forms such as crookle (and variants) with meanings in the same semantic field — to bend, make crooked, stoop, hobble — senses that naturally extend to tripping, stumbling or going over on a foot. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect material and comparative work on Germanic vocabularies point to a family of related words (crook‑, kruk‑ types) across northern English and Scots dialects and into Scandinavian dialects; the picture is of an old verb pattern that local communities have kept alive in different forms.

The Dictionary of the Scots Language and related dialect sources list cognate forms (cruggle, cruckle, krukel, etc.) meaning to crouch, bend or huddle; the entries show how frequentative or imitative verb endings (‑le) and the crook/krug root produce senses of bending, stooping and halting movement. In short: linguists see cruckle as a predictable local survival of a wider, older dialect verb group rather than a completely isolated coinage.

Is cruckle unique to Rochdale? It depends how you look at it. On the one hand, folk‑linguistic evidence — what people say about accents and vocabulary — strongly ties the word to Rochdale: residents and others in the region often point to it as a local marker. On the other hand, dialect records show related forms elsewhere in northern England and in Scots dialects, so the root is regional rather than absolutely exclusive. What makes the word feel particularly “Rochdale” is the combination of continued local use, local recognition, and the way people use it as an emblem of home speech.

Why do dialect researchers care? Small words like cruckle are useful because they reveal two things at once: living speech practice (who still uses the word and where) and folk awareness (which terms people think define their place). Modern perceptual studies use crowd‑sourced mapping and keyword analysis to show where labels cluster and how they carry social meaning — for Rochdale, cruckle is one of those small but telling signals of local identity.

If you’re after a short take‑away: the word’s meaning — to roll or twist your ankle — matches local usage in Rochdale today; its form is part of a long‑standing northern dialect family (crookle/cruckle/kruggle); and research shows it is especially strongly associated with Rochdale in people’s perceptions, even while related forms appear elsewhere in historical records. If you don’t know the word, try using it next time you take a tumble in a ginnel — you’ll probably get a nod of recognition from someone from round here.

Note on sources: this piece draws on recent perceptual dialect research into Greater Manchester (Dann et al., Journal of Linguistic Geography, 2024), historical dialect lexicography and Scots dialect entries that document related forms, and reporting of the British Library’s dialect collecting work that records cruckle/crookle among regionally attested words.

articles.title: Ignite Fire Festival Returns to Rochdale from November 20-22, 2026
articles.excerpt: The Ignite Fire Festival will return to Rochdale Town Hall for three nights of entertainment, featuring new displays and the Christmas lights switch-on.
articles.content_html:
The Ignite Fire Festival is set to return to Rochdale from Friday, November 20, to Sunday, November 22, 2026. Organised by Rochdale Development Agency, the festival promises three evenings of magical family entertainment, featuring new displays and attractions that will transform the square and gardens around Rochdale Town Hall.

Following the success of its inaugural event in 2023, which attracted over 10,000 attendees, this year's festival will include immersive trails of fire, lights, and sound. Visitors can expect to walk through fiery displays, blazing sculptures, and an illuminated installation created by the award-winning outdoor arts specialists Walk the Plank. The festival will also feature a performance called 'Fireflies', showcasing local talent from Rochdale’s Skylight Circus Arts and Travelling Light Circus.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, expressed excitement about the festival's return, stating that it has quickly become one of the most popular events in the borough. She encouraged families to mark their calendars for what promises to be an unforgettable experience, coinciding with the official Christmas lights switch-on on the final evening.

The festival is funded by Rochdale Borough Council, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority's Flexible Fund, and in partnership with Walk the Plank and Culture Co-op. Further details about the event will be available next month on the Rochdale Council website.
